prog-csp-001.question: You are implanting a left bundle branch area pacing lead. Despite several rotations, the lead no longer advances. Unipolar pacing from the tip gives a narrower QRS than RV septal pacing, with no notching in the left lateral leads, but there is no terminal R wave in V1 and no criterion of conduction system capture. According to the 2023 EHRA consensus, how should this pacing be classified?
options: Deep septal pacing (DSP)
Left ventricular septal pacing (LVSP)
Left fascicular pacing (LFP)
Non-selective His bundle pacing
commentaires: Correct: the lead is deep in the septum without reaching the LV subendocardium, the QRS is narrower than with RV septal pacing, and there is neither a terminal R wave in V1 nor any criterion of conduction system capture.
Incorrect: LVSP implies that the lead has reached the left side of the septum; it produces a terminal R wave in V1.
Incorrect: LFP requires criteria of conduction system capture, often with an axis that differs from the native axis.
Incorrect: the lead is screwed into the ventricular septum, far from the His region, and the QRS does not have the features of His bundle capture.
prog-csp-001.explication: The 2023 EHRA consensus distinguishes several entities. Deep septal pacing (DSP) refers to a lead driven into the septum without reaching the LV subendocardium: the QRS is narrower than with RV septal pacing and has no lateral notching, but there is no terminal R wave in V1 and no criterion of left conduction system capture. It often results from failure to advance the lead to the left side of the septum. LBBAP encompasses left bundle branch pacing (LBBP), left fascicular pacing (LFP) and left ventricular septal pacing (LVSP), the latter being recognised by a terminal R wave in V1 without any criterion of conduction system capture. Beware: a few genuine LBBAP cases have no terminal R wave in V1 (relatively early RV activation); the other criteria then settle the question.
prog-csp-001.aRetenir: Deep lead, narrower QRS but no terminal R wave in V1 and no conduction system criterion: this is deep septal pacing, not LBBAP.

prog-csp-002.question: According to the 2023 EHRA consensus, which landmarks are proposed to choose the insertion site and orientation of an LBBAP lead? (select all that apply)
options: In 20–30° RAO, target an area about 15–35 mm from the top of the tricuspid annulus or the His potential
In 30–40° LAO, angle the lead about 10–40° upwards from the horizontal, perpendicular to the septum
On initial pacing of the right septum, preferably look for a dominant R wave in V1
Aim for the RV apex, where the left bundle branch is most superficial
In LAO, angle the lead downwards, parallel to the septum, so as not to cross it
commentaires: Correct: the area 15–35 mm from the top of the tricuspid annulus (or the His) in 20–30° RAO is the proposed starting landmark.
Correct: the 30–40° LAO view is used to check that the lead is perpendicular to the septum, typically 20–30° above the horizontal.
Incorrect: a good initial site instead shows a "W" pattern in V1 (notch at the nadir), with II positive or isoelectric and III negative.
Incorrect: the left bundle branch runs along the left side of the basal to mid septum, not at the RV apex.
Incorrect: the lead must enter the septum perpendicularly; a parallel orientation prevents it from advancing.
prog-csp-002.explication: Because the left bundle branch cannot be mapped directly from the RV, the 2023 EHRA consensus relies on indirect landmarks. In 20–30° RAO, the His or the top of the tricuspid annulus is identified, then the sheath is advanced towards the apex to target an area about 15–35 mm from that point, on the basal to mid septum. In 30–40° LAO, the lead should be perpendicular to the septum, angled 10–40° (often 20–30°) above the horizontal. Unipolar pacing of the right septum before screwing in helps: a "W" pattern in V1 with II positive and III negative indicates a good site (concordant polarities in II and III can also succeed, at the expense of reaching the anterior or posterior fascicular region). A site that is too basal carries a higher risk of worsening tricuspid regurgitation.
prog-csp-002.aRetenir: LBBAP: area 15–35 mm from the top of the tricuspid annulus in RAO, lead perpendicular to the septum (10–40° upwards) in LAO, "W" pattern in V1 at the start.

prog-csp-003.question: While screwing in an LBBAP lead, which signs indicate that the tip is approaching the left subendocardium and that rotations should be paused to test the capture criteria? (select all that apply)
options: Fixation beats with a QR or rSR' pattern in V1
A fall in unipolar myocardial current of injury after an initial rise
A progressive lengthening of the V6 R-wave peak time with each rotation
Appearance of a terminal R wave in V1 on the paced QRS
A sudden rise in unipolar impedance
commentaires: Correct: fixation beats reflect the depth of the tip; a QR/rSR' pattern in V1 signals that the left bundle branch area has been reached.
Correct: the current of injury first rises (to around 20–35 mV) and then falls when the lead reaches the left subendocardium.
Incorrect: the opposite occurs; the V6 R-wave peak time shortens as the lead advances towards the left.
Correct: the terminal R wave in V1 reflects delayed RV activation; this is the moment to stop and test the criteria.
Incorrect: impedance rises and then falls as the LV is approached; a sudden rise instead suggests helix retraction on a stylet-driven lead.
prog-csp-003.explication: No single landmark is sufficient: the 2023 EHRA consensus recommends combining several methods. During continuous unipolar pacing, the QRS narrows, loses its notching and takes on a Qr/qR/rsR' pattern in V1 while the V6 R-wave peak time shortens. Fixation beats (mechanical ectopy) have a morphology close to that of the paced QRS at the same depth: a QR/rSR' pattern in V1 heralds the left bundle branch area. Unipolar impedance rises and then falls as the LV endocardium is approached; caution is needed at around 500 Ω or after a 200 Ω drop. The current of injury also falls, to around 10–12 mV; a marked drop, to about 5 mV, calls for even greater caution. Fluoroscopy alone cannot assess depth.
prog-csp-003.aRetenir: Stop screwing as soon as a terminal R wave appears in V1, QR/rSR' fixation beats occur or the current of injury falls, then test the capture criteria.

prog-csp-004.question: LBBAP with a lumenless lead. After two extra rotations "to lower the threshold", unipolar impedance falls from 720 to 420 Ω. The tip current of injury is now only 2 mV, lower than that of the ring, with a QS pattern. Capture persists at 1.7 V. What should be done?
options: Leave the lead in place, since capture is still achieved
Unscrew one or two turns, then recheck the current of injury
Reposition the lead at a new site on the septum
Add two more rotations to anchor the helix better
commentaires: Incorrect: persistent capture does not rule out a septal perforation (partial or complete).
Incorrect: the consensus advises against simply withdrawing the lead, because the tunnel created predisposes to dislodgement.
Correct: intraprocedural septal perforation is managed by repositioning the lead at a new site.
Incorrect: further screwing would worsen the perforation.
prog-csp-004.explication: This picture combines several markers of septal perforation listed in the 2023 EHRA consensus: a collapsed unipolar current of injury (below 3–5 mV, or below 25% of the V EGM amplitude), a ring current of injury greater than that of the tip, a QS or RS morphology, and impedance falling below 450 Ω with the 3830 lead (or by more than 200 Ω). Capture may still be possible with a microperforation, as the helix remains partly in contact with excitable tissue. The lead should then be repositioned at a new site rather than backed out a few turns: the tunnel created ("drill" effect) predisposes to late dislodgement. Once the lead is repositioned, acute perforation is asymptomatic and has no known sequelae.
prog-csp-004.aRetenir: Collapsed current of injury, ring > tip, impedance < 450 Ω: septal perforation, managed by repositioning the lead at another site.

prog-csp-005.question: A CT scan performed some time after LBBAP shows the tip of the helix slightly exposed in the LV cavity (microperforation). Thresholds and sensing are low and stable. True or false: long-term oral anticoagulation is indicated to prevent embolism.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: for a microperforation with stable parameters, the consensus recommends neither reintervention nor long-term anticoagulation.
Correct: no stroke has been attributed to this situation, probably thanks to rapid endothelialisation; anticoagulation is only discussed for a late complete perforation, pending lead repositioning.
prog-csp-005.explication: Microperforation is probably underestimated, as septal thickness varies considerably. When it is found on imaging with low, stable thresholds, the 2023 EHRA consensus does not consider reintervention justified. The embolic risk remains theoretical: no stroke has been attributed to it, probably owing to rapid endothelialisation, and long-term anticoagulation is not indicated. Late complete septal perforation (about 0.1 to 0.3% of cases) is a different matter: it is managed by repositioning the lead, with oral anticoagulation if the procedure is delayed.
prog-csp-005.aRetenir: Microperforation with stable parameters: neither reintervention nor anticoagulation; late complete perforation: reposition the lead (and anticoagulate if the procedure is delayed).

prog-csp-006.question: During LBBAP, the operator rotates the lead many times. On fluoroscopy, the lead no longer advances and the paced QRS does not change. No torque build-up is felt. Which phenomenon is involved, and what is its risk?
options: "Screwdriver" effect: no risk, normal advancement
"Drill" effect: tunnel without anchoring, risk of dislodgement
Endocardial entanglement: risk of damaging the helix
Helix retraction: risk of immediate perforation
commentaires: Incorrect: the screwdriver effect is the steady advancement that is sought; here the lead is not advancing.
Correct: the lead spins in place and bores a tunnel without the helix anchoring, with a risk of micro- or macrodislodgement.
Incorrect: endocardial entanglement causes marked torque build-up from the very first turns.
Incorrect: helix retraction (stylet-driven lead) is recognised by a sudden rise in impedance and by fluoroscopic landmarks.
prog-csp-006.explication: The 2023 EHRA consensus describes three lead behaviours during septal penetration. The "screwdriver" effect is the steady advancement being sought. Entanglement shows as marked torque build-up from the first turns: the lead is unlikely to penetrate and may be damaged if the operator persists. The "drill" effect corresponds to many rotations without progress, either on fluoroscopy or on pacing: a tunnel forms without the helix anchoring, with a risk of dislodgement. The operator should then change site or increase forward pressure and sheath support before continuing. Both the screwdriver and drill effects can lead to perforation if depth is not monitored.
prog-csp-006.aRetenir: Rotations without progress = "drill" effect: risk of dislodgement; change site or improve sheath support.

prog-csp-007.question: Decremental unipolar threshold test just after fixation of an LBBAP lead. When going from 1 V to 0.9 V at 0.5 ms, the QRS measured from the spike widens, V1 changes from qR to rsR' with a rounded R' wave, and the S wave deepens in I and V6. The V6 R-wave peak time remains 70 ms. On the lead EGM, a discrete local ventricular potential appears after the spike. How should this transition be interpreted?
options: Loss of left bundle capture, change to LV septal pacing
Loss of anodal ring capture, of no consequence
Change from His bundle capture to right bundle capture
Non-selective then selective left bundle branch capture
commentaires: Incorrect: loss of left bundle branch capture prolongs the V6 R-wave peak time (≥ 15 ms), without changing the local signal.
Incorrect: the test is unipolar, with no anode on the ring; and the local EGM shows loss of capture of the myocardium in contact with the tip.
Incorrect: the lead is screwed into the ventricular septum, and the short, stable V6 R-wave peak time reflects rapid left-sided activation.
Correct: the septal myocardium is no longer captured but the left bundle branch still is: wider QRS, unchanged V6 timing, discrete local potential.
prog-csp-007.explication: Just after fixation, the myocardial threshold is transiently raised by the current of injury: this is the best time to unmask a transition. When capture changes from non-selective to selective left bundle branch capture, the QRS widens (measured from the spike), V1 takes on an rsR' pattern with a rounded R' and a longer V1 R-wave peak time, the S wave deepens in I/V6, but the V6 R-wave peak time does not change. On the EGM, a discrete local ventricular potential appears: the local myocardium is no longer captured. Conversely, a change to LV septal pacing (loss of bundle capture) prolongs the V6 R-wave peak time, reduces the terminal R wave in V1 and abolishes the S wave in I/V6, without changing the local EGM. Selective capture, rarely seen at follow-up, confirms conduction system capture.
prog-csp-007.aRetenir: ns-LBBP → s-LBBP: wider QRS, rounded R' in V1, unchanged V6 timing, discrete local potential on the EGM; ns-LBBP → LVSP: longer V6 R-wave peak time.

prog-csp-008.question: True or false: to demonstrate left bundle branch capture with a decremental threshold test, pacing should be unipolar, because in bipolar configuration anodal capture by the ring can create a misleading morphology transition.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: the 2023 EHRA consensus recommends a unipolar test; a transition due to anodal capture does not prove conduction system capture.

Incorrect: the ring, lying in the right septum, can capture the myocardium at high output in bipolar configuration; losing this capture changes the QRS for reasons unrelated to the left bundle branch.
prog-csp-008.explication: The decremental threshold test (from 5–10 V at 0.5 ms down to loss of capture) is the recommended first-line method to demonstrate left bundle branch capture. It must be performed in unipolar configuration: in bipolar mode, the ring can capture the right septal myocardium (anodal capture), and loss of this capture changes the QRS for reasons unrelated to the left bundle branch. If anodal capture is observed, it should be documented along with its threshold; it may even shorten the QRS. This is why the consensus advises comparing QRS width in unipolar and bipolar configurations at follow-up. The absence of a transition does not disprove capture: the bundle branch and myocardial thresholds may be almost identical.
prog-csp-008.aRetenir: LBBAP threshold test in unipolar configuration: in bipolar mode, anodal capture can create a false transition.

prog-csp-009.question: LBBAP in a patient with complete AV block and a wide escape rhythm. During the unipolar threshold test, the V6 R-wave peak time is 74 ms from 5 V down to 0.7 V, then abruptly increases to 96 ms at 0.6 V with a subtle change in the QRS, before loss of capture at 0.3 V. What is the interpretation?
options: Loss of left bundle capture at 0.6 V: bundle threshold of 0.7 V
Loss of myocardial capture: selective left bundle branch pacing
Meaningless measurement variation, within the variability range
Anodal ring capture appearing at low output
commentaires: Correct: an abrupt increase of ≥ 15 ms in the V6 R-wave peak time as output is reduced indicates loss of left bundle branch capture.
Incorrect: the change to selective capture does not alter the V6 R-wave peak time.
Incorrect: measurement variability is about 12 ms; a 22 ms jump exceeds this.
Incorrect: the test is unipolar, and anodal capture appears at high output, not at low output.
prog-csp-009.explication: The V6 R-wave peak time reflects activation of the LV lateral wall. As long as the left bundle branch is captured, it remains short and constant. If it abruptly increases by at least 15 ms when output is reduced, bundle branch capture has been lost (sensitivity about 83%, specificity 100% in the reference study): only the septal myocardium remains captured. The 2023 EHRA consensus prefers this 15 ms cut-off to the 10 ms cut-off, which lies within the interobserver variability (about 12 ms). Here, the left bundle branch capture threshold is therefore 0.7 V and the myocardial threshold 0.4 V; the safety margin should be based on the bundle branch threshold. The other QRS changes may be very subtle, hence the value of measuring V6 with electronic callipers.
prog-csp-009.aRetenir: An abrupt jump of ≥ 15 ms in the V6 R-wave peak time as output is reduced = loss of left bundle branch capture.

prog-csp-010.question: According to the 2023 EHRA consensus, which intraprocedural results are acceptable? (select all that apply)
options: LBBAP: capture threshold of 0.8 V at 0.5 ms
LBBAP: capture threshold of 2.2 V at 0.5 ms
His: threshold of 1.2 V at 0.5 ms, bipolar R wave of 3 mV without oversensing
His: bipolar R wave of 1 mV with His oversensing, in complete AV block
commentaires: Correct: for LBBAP, the threshold should be < 1.5 V at 0.5 ms, ideally < 1 V.
Incorrect: 2.2 V exceeds the acceptable LBBAP threshold of 1.5 V at 0.5 ms; the position should be revised (after allowing the current of injury to settle).
Correct: for His bundle pacing, a threshold ≤ 1.5 V at 0.5 ms is optimal and the bipolar R wave should exceed 2 mV, without atrial or His oversensing.
Incorrect: a small R wave with His oversensing is dangerous in complete AV block (inhibition); a more distal site or an RV backup lead for sensing is needed.
prog-csp-010.explication: Requirements differ between the two techniques. For LBBAP, the capture threshold should be below 1.5 V at 0.5 ms (ideally below 1 V), with a bipolar R wave ideally above 4 mV. For His bundle pacing, a threshold ≤ 1.5 V at 0.5 ms is optimal; up to 2.0–2.5 V is tolerated in some settings (heart failure, only resynchronisation option), with a bipolar R wave above 2 mV (or unipolar above 4 mV). With non-selective His capture, His and myocardial thresholds should be documented separately. An initially high threshold may be due to the current of injury: it should be rechecked after a few minutes. Atrial or His oversensing is potentially fatal in a patient with complete AV block.
prog-csp-010.aRetenir: LBBAP: threshold < 1.5 V (ideally < 1 V) at 0.5 ms, R wave > 4 mV; His: threshold ≤ 1.5 V optimal (≤ 2.5 V tolerated), R wave > 2 mV without oversensing.

prog-csp-011.question: His bundle pacing: after five rotations, the His capture threshold is 1.9 V at 0.5 ms. The unfiltered unipolar EGM shows neither a His current of injury nor inversion of the His potential. What does the 2023 EHRA consensus recommend?
options: Accept it: the threshold is within the tolerated range at 0.5 ms
Lengthen the pulse width to 1 ms to lower the threshold
Keep rotating until a His current of injury appears
Withdraw the sheath and remeasure in ten minutes
commentaires: Incorrect: without a current of injury, contact with the His bundle is probably inadequate, with a risk of instability and late threshold rise.
Incorrect: this masks the problem without improving lead contact with the His bundle.
Correct: further rotations, until clear torque build-up, often bring out a current of injury and a negative His potential, both predictive of a good threshold.
Incorrect: waiting is useful when a current of injury transiently raises the threshold, not when there is none.
prog-csp-011.explication: The His bundle is surrounded by fibrous tissue: recording its potential guarantees neither contact nor capture. According to the 2023 EHRA consensus, it is torque build-up, not the number of turns, that indicates good fixation. The operator should then look for a His current of injury and/or inversion of the His potential (which becomes negative). If these signs are absent, rotations should be resumed, aiming for greater torque: the signs then often appear, with a marked improvement in threshold. A lead with poor contact is prone to instability and late threshold rise. Conversely, when a His current of injury is present, the threshold may be transiently high: it should be rechecked every five minutes. Measurements are made with the sheath withdrawn a few centimetres, so as not to underestimate the threshold.
prog-csp-011.aRetenir: His bundle pacing: keep rotating until a His current of injury or a negative His potential appears, both predictive of a good, durable threshold.

prog-csp-012.question: A pacemaker-dependent patient (complete AV block) has a His bundle pacing lead with no backup RV lead. The His capture threshold is high. You want to favour non-selective capture, to keep backup myocardial capture. Which pulse width setting helps achieve this?
options: Shorten the pulse width to 0.2–0.3 ms
Keep 0.4 ms and program the amplitude at twice the threshold
Lengthen the pulse width to 1.0–1.5 ms
Switch to bipolar to capture via the ring
commentaires: Incorrect: short pulses widen the window of selective capture, i.e. without myocardial capture.
Incorrect: this ignores the divergence between the His and myocardial strength–duration curves, which can be exploited.
Correct: at long pulse widths, His and myocardial thresholds converge, favouring simultaneous capture of both.
Incorrect: anodal ring capture remains unpredictable and is not the proposed strategy.
prog-csp-012.explication: The chronaxie of the His bundle is shorter than that of the adjacent ventricular myocardium: their strength–duration curves diverge at short pulse widths. Short pulses (0.2–0.3 ms) therefore widen the window of selective capture. This is useful when the QRS with non-selective capture is too wide, and also to unmask a transition during threshold testing. Conversely, long pulses (1.0–1.5 ms) bring the two thresholds closer and facilitate non-selective capture. This is desirable in a pacemaker-dependent patient or when the His threshold is high, because myocardial capture acts as a backup. The 2023 EHRA consensus considers selective and non-selective capture clinically equivalent, non-selective capture being safer and offering better sensing.
prog-csp-012.aRetenir: His: short pulse (0.2–0.3 ms) favours selective capture; long pulse (1–1.5 ms) favours non-selective capture, which is safer in pacemaker-dependent patients.

prog-csp-013.question: His bundle pacing in a patient with a prolonged HV interval (infranodal block). His capture is confirmed at the programmed output. Which additional test does the 2023 EHRA consensus require before accepting this site?
options: Atrial pacing up to the AV nodal Wenckebach point
1:1 conduction during His pacing at cycle lengths ≤ 400 ms
An atropine test to locate the level of block
An early exercise test before the patient is discharged
commentaires: Incorrect: the Wenckebach point assesses the AV node, proximal to the His pacing site.
Correct: His capture with 1:1 conduction must be demonstrated at cycle lengths ≤ 400 ms, without aberrancy.
Incorrect: atropine acts mainly on the AV node and does not test conduction distal to the pacing site.
Incorrect: the consensus requires an intraprocedural pacing test, not an exercise test.
prog-csp-013.explication: In the presence of infranodal delay or block, His bundle pacing is only useful if the site is distal to the lesion. The 2023 EHRA consensus therefore requires demonstration, at the programmed output, of His capture with 1:1 conduction at cycle lengths ≤ 400 ms. If block appears during incremental pacing (loss of ventricular capture, or a QRS that widens with notching and loss of His capture criteria), the site is at or proximal to the lesion and a more distal site should be sought. In this setting, a backup ventricular lead should also be considered (infranodal block, class IIa recommendation in the 2021 ESC guidelines).
prog-csp-013.aRetenir: Infranodal block: require 1:1 conduction at ≤ 400 ms during His pacing; otherwise, look for a more distal site.

prog-csp-014.question: A patient with permanent AF is a candidate for His bundle pacing followed by AV junction ablation. True or false: a His site with a large atrial EGM (> 0.5 mV) is preferred, as this proximal site gives a better threshold.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: a proximal His site, close to the future ablation target, is at risk of a rise in His threshold after ablation.
Correct: the consensus advises avoiding sites with an atrial EGM > 0.5 mV and aiming for a more distal His site, away from the junction to be ablated.
prog-csp-014.explication: When AV junction ablation is planned, the His lead must be placed away from the ablation site. A site with a large atrial EGM (> 0.5 mV) is proximal, close to the AV node: ablation may raise the His capture threshold there. In AF, rapid atrial signals can also mimic His potentials: mapping can be started on the ventricular side of the membranous septum. Planned AV junction ablation is one of the situations in which the 2021 ESC guidelines suggest a backup RV lead. The 2023 EHRA consensus notes that with LBBAP, ablation can be performed without risk of compromising lead function.
prog-csp-014.aRetenir: His lead before AV junction ablation: avoid sites with a large atrial EGM (> 0.5 mV), which are too close to the ablation target.

prog-csp-015.question: True or false: in a patient with His bundle pacing, in-person follow-up every six months is advised, because late threshold rises are common and automatic capture tests are unreliable in this setting.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: the 2021 ESC guidelines, echoed by the 2023 EHRA consensus, advise in-person visits every six months for His bundle pacing, with a 12-lead ECG.
Incorrect: late threshold rise (loss of His capture in up to 17% of patients) and the limitations of capture algorithms justify this close follow-up.
prog-csp-015.explication: The most common complication of His bundle pacing is a rise in threshold, with loss of His capture in up to 17% of patients or lead revision in up to 11%. Automatic threshold measurement algorithms are unreliable with a His lead. The 2021 ESC guidelines therefore recommend in-person follow-up every six months; each visit includes a paced 12-lead ECG to check His capture and bundle branch block correction. His capture, bundle branch block correction and myocardial thresholds are documented separately, and absence of atrial oversensing is checked. With LBBAP, as thresholds are low and stable, follow-up can be less frequent and rely more on remote monitoring if the device measures the threshold reliably.
prog-csp-015.aRetenir: His bundle pacing: in-person follow-up every six months with a 12-lead ECG; LBBAP allows less frequent follow-up.

prog-csp-016.question: Proximal His bundle pacing (atrial side of the tricuspid annulus) in a patient with complete AV block. The His lead is connected to the RV port. Which statements about sensing are correct? (select all that apply)
options: Atrial or His oversensing can inhibit pacing, with a life-threatening risk in complete AV block
If sensing is borderline on the PSA, it should be rechecked once the lead is connected to the device
A 1.5 mV bipolar R wave is sufficient, since His capture is selective
A more proximal site usually improves R-wave amplitude
LBBAP causes more ventricular sensing problems than His pacing
commentaires: Correct: on the RV port, a sensed atrial or His EGM is interpreted as a ventricular event and inhibits pacing.
Correct: the device filters differ from those of the PSA; borderline values should be rechecked on the device.
Incorrect: the bipolar R wave should ideally exceed 2 mV; otherwise, use a more distal site or a dedicated RV sensing lead.
Incorrect: a more distal site, on the ventricular side of the annulus, gives a better R wave and less oversensing.
Incorrect: on the contrary, LBBAP provides good sensing (bipolar R wave ideally > 4 mV).
prog-csp-016.explication: Sensing requires much more attention with His bundle pacing than with conventional RV pacing. In a proximal position, on the atrial side of the annulus, capture is often selective, but the R wave is small and the atrial or His EGM may be oversensed. On the ventricular port, this oversensing inhibits pacing, which can be fatal in a patient with complete AV block. The 2023 EHRA consensus requires a bipolar R wave > 2 mV (unipolar > 4 mV) without oversensing. Otherwise, a more distal site is tried or an RV lead is added for sensing, often connected to the RV port. Borderline values on the PSA must be rechecked on the device, whose filters differ. Absence of atrial oversensing is also checked at every follow-up.
prog-csp-016.aRetenir: His lead on the RV port: bipolar R wave > 2 mV, no atrial/His oversensing (risk of inhibition in complete AV block), borderline values rechecked on the device.

prog-csp-017.question: LBBAP with a stylet-driven lead with an extendable-retractable helix, with continuous unipolar pacing via the stylet. While rotating the lead body, the impedance suddenly rises, whereas the paced QRS does not change. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The tip has reached the left subendocardium
Septal perforation with the tip in the LV cavity
Contact of the helix with the left bundle branch
Retraction of the helix into the lead body
commentaires: Incorrect: as the left subendocardium is approached, impedance falls after its initial rise.
Incorrect: perforation causes impedance to fall (below 450 Ω or by more than 200 Ω).
Incorrect: no impedance profile indicates contact with the bundle branch; this is judged from the ECG and potentials.
Correct: the lead body can rotate around the inner coil and retract the helix, causing impedance to rise.
prog-csp-017.explication: Stylet-driven leads differ from lumenless leads (3830): they have a larger diameter, are stiffer with the stylet in place, and their helix is usually extendable-retractable. When the lead body is rotated, it can turn around the inner coil and retract the helix. This is recognised by a sudden rise in impedance and by the radio-opaque markers. To prevent it, the inner coil is pre-tensioned with a few extra turns of the connector pin before it is locked. The stylet allows continuous unipolar pacing during fixation. The stylet and sheath should be partially withdrawn before measuring thresholds, and the stylet pulled back about 10 cm while the sheath is slit, so as not to dislodge the lead.
prog-csp-017.aRetenir: Stylet-driven lead for LBBAP: a sudden rise in impedance during fixation suggests helix retraction, prevented by pre-tensioning the inner coil.

prog-csp-018.question: A patient with complete LBBB and preserved AV conduction is referred for LBBAP. Why does the 2023 EHRA consensus advise placing a temporary pacing lead before implanting the conduction system lead?
options: To act as a fluoroscopic landmark for the His bundle
To measure the patient's VA conduction time before implanting the lead
To be able to deliver a shock if VF occurs
Because right bundle trauma can cause complete AV block
commentaires: Incorrect: the His landmark can be provided by the lead itself, or by a second lead in the two-lead technique, not by a temporary lead.
Incorrect: VA conduction is not the reason; the risk is asystole due to bilateral bundle branch block.
Incorrect: a temporary pacing lead does not deliver shocks.
Correct: with pre-existing LBBB, traumatic right bundle branch block during the procedure leaves the patient without AV conduction.
prog-csp-018.explication: Manipulating the sheath and lead near the His bundle and septum can injure the right bundle branch, usually transiently. In a patient who already has LBBB, or a wide junctional escape rhythm, this trauma can cause complete AV block. The 2023 EHRA consensus therefore advises considering a temporary pacing lead, connected to an additional PSA or an external pacemaker. If a defibrillation lead is planned, it is implanted first; if an atrial lead is planned, it can be placed temporarily in the RV. In the study by Chen et al., 10 of the 49 patients undergoing LBBP-CRT had right bundle branch trauma, 9 of whom recovered before discharge.
prog-csp-018.aRetenir: LBBB or wide escape rhythm: temporary backup pacing before CSP, because right bundle branch trauma can cause complete AV block.

prog-csp-019.question: The study by Chen et al. (Europace 2022) compared, in 100 patients with HFrEF and typical LBBB, resynchronisation by left bundle branch pacing (LBBP-CRT) with biventricular pacing using an adaptive algorithm. The LBBP-CRT group had a higher LVEF and more super-responders. Which limitation prevents concluding that LBBP is superior?
options: Patients did not have LBBB according to Strauss criteria
Follow-up, limited to one month, was too short
Non-randomised groups; surrogate echocardiographic endpoints
Mortality was higher in the LBBP-CRT group
commentaires: Incorrect: on the contrary, typical LBBB according to Strauss criteria, with QRS ≥ 150 ms, was an inclusion criterion.
Incorrect: follow-up lasted one year, with no loss to follow-up.
Correct: the technique was chosen by shared decision-making between operator and patient, with a risk of selection bias, and the endpoints were surrogate.
Incorrect: there were no deaths, and HF hospitalisations did not differ significantly.
prog-csp-019.explication: This prospective multicentre study was observational: allocation between LBBP-CRT (49 patients) and optimised biventricular pacing (51) was based on shared decision-making, without randomisation. It showed a narrower QRS, a lower and stable threshold, a higher LVEF and more super-responders with LBBP, with no difference in responder rate or HF hospitalisations. A further caveat is that most patients in the LBBP group also received an LV lead. Subsequent small randomised trials (e.g. LBBP-RESYNC) confirmed an LVEF benefit, again on surrogate endpoints. The 2025 ESC/EHRA consensus considers CSP-CRT a possible alternative to biventricular CRT in LBBB with LVEF ≤ 35%. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines make no recommendation, in the absence of trials with clinical endpoints.
prog-csp-019.aRetenir: LBBP-CRT: promising data, but observational or based on surrogate endpoints; no 2026 ESC recommendation, in the absence of trials with clinical endpoints.

prog-csp-020.question: Left bundle branch pacing for resynchronisation in a patient in sinus rhythm with LBBB, a PR interval of 170 ms and preserved right bundle conduction. With LBBP alone (VVI), the paced QRS measures 122 ms, with a right-sided delay pattern. Which setting usually narrows it further?
options: A very short AV delay, for complete pre-excitation
An AV delay adjusted for fusion with right bundle conduction
Additional RV apical pacing with a VV delay of zero
VVI mode at 70 bpm to abolish AV conduction
commentaires: Incorrect: complete pre-excitation keeps the right-sided delay pattern, because the RV is still activated across the septum.
Correct: if the right bundle conducts, an appropriate AV delay fuses RV activation via intrinsic conduction with left-sided pacing.
Incorrect: RV apical pacing adds a non-physiological activation wavefront and is not the strategy used.
Incorrect: VVI mode abolishes AV synchrony, and the right-sided delay pattern persists.
prog-csp-020.explication: LBBP activates the LV rapidly, but the RV is activated later, across the septum: hence the pseudo-right bundle branch delay pattern. When the right bundle conducts normally and the PR interval is not too long, an AV delay can be programmed so that left-sided pacing coincides with RV activation via intrinsic conduction. This gives the narrowest QRS, guided by the ECG. In the study by Chen et al. (patients with PR > 200 ms excluded), this fusion reduced the paced QRS from about 121 ms in VVI to about 103 ms, with a mean AV delay of 112 ms. In cases of traumatic RBBB during implantation, the authors added LV or RV pacing with an 80 ms offset, then reverted to LBBP alone once the right bundle had recovered.
prog-csp-020.aRetenir: LBBP with a conducting right bundle: adjust the AV delay on the ECG to achieve fusion with right-sided conduction and abolish the pseudo-right bundle branch delay.

prog-csp-021.question: Three-month follow-up after LBBAP for complete AV block. Telemetered thresholds are satisfactory. On the paced 12-lead ECG, the terminal R wave in V1 present at discharge has disappeared, and the QRS has widened with a longer V6 R-wave peak time. Which hypothesis should be considered first?
options: Return of intrinsic AV conduction with fusion
Normal maturation of the lead–tissue interface
Anodal capture emerging with maturation
Lead pull-back: loss of left-sided capture
commentaires: Incorrect: fusion would tend to narrow the QRS; it would not explain a wider QRS with a longer V6 R-wave peak time.
Incorrect: maturation alters the threshold, not the morphology of the QRS captured at the same site.
Incorrect: anodal capture by the ring tends to shorten the QRS.
Correct: disappearance of the terminal R wave in V1 suggests microdislodgement of the lead towards the right septum, with loss of left-sided capture.
prog-csp-021.explication: Lead microdislodgement with loss of left bundle branch capture is probably underestimated. In the MELOS registry, the terminal R wave in V1 disappeared during follow-up in 4% of patients. Satisfactory telemetered thresholds are not enough, as the lead can capture the right septal myocardium at a low threshold: the diagnosis is made on the 12-lead ECG, which is mandatory at in-person follow-up. Compare with the discharge ECG: same V1 pattern, same V6 R-wave peak time. The consensus also advises recording the potential-to-V6 R-wave peak interval in the implant report to facilitate this follow-up. The decision to reposition is made case by case.
prog-csp-021.aRetenir: At LBBAP follow-up, loss of the terminal R wave in V1 with a longer V6 R-wave peak time suggests microdislodgement: the 12-lead ECG is essential.
